title: The Ingredient That Wasn’t There
angle: A recipe’s substitutions show how cultural continuity depends less on exact ingredients than on the judgment that carries a dish forward.
paragraphs: A recipe card may call for a particular kind of bean, while the pot on the stove contains a different one. The change might come from what the shop had, what the cook preferred, or what needed using up. On the page, it looks like a small departure. At the table, it may be the version everyone recognizes.

Recipes are often treated as instructions for reproducing an original. But they can also record a series of practical decisions: which flavor matters, what can be swapped, how much heat feels right. The exact ingredient list is only part of the knowledge. The rest lives in judgment, including the judgment that a dish can survive a change.

That doesn’t mean every alteration is equally meaningful, or that origins stop mattering. Knowing where a dish comes from can deepen the pleasure of making it. Still, continuity need not mean keeping every detail untouched. A kitchen is not a museum case; it is a place where the next meal has to be made with what is available.

The interesting question may be not whether a recipe has changed, but which parts people choose to carry forward. Sometimes a tradition lasts because someone knew what could be different without losing what made it worth making.
